She selected algae because their thin, branching forms could be flattened onto paper without losing their distinctive shapes. Although algae live in water, some species can survive brief periods of drying. Rather than relying on a commercial printer, Atkins produced each page by hand and arranged the specimens carefully. This hand-production meant that every page in her books was made by hand.

She often added handwritten labels to identify each specimen by its scientific name. Some copies had pages that differed from one another because the specimens and exposures varied. The blue color of cyanotypes later became popular in architectural drawings. Atkins's books therefore functioned as both scientific records and works of visual art.
